utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Alexis Demirdjian for the Prosecution, with Douglas Stringer; our case manager, Indah Susanti; as well as our legal intern, Robert Goodwin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are pleased to see you back, Mr. Zivanovic. We hope you are well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Witness 080, the witness may be brought in, in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you, sir. We will start cross-examination now. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and in these proceedings I represent Goran Hadzic. I am going to put some questions to you, and they all stem from the testimony you provided yesterday and the day before yesterday. I'll start with the period leading up to the beginning of armed conflicts in Vukovar. You said that in 1984 you served in the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, would you just please confirm whether I'm right, you were given a war assignment in case there was a war or a military maneuver? After you served in the army, you were assigned to an assignment?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed, as a matter of fact, that at one point you said that you were a reservist together with a colleague of yours with whom we are not going to name. That's why I put that question to you. I thought that you were a member of a reserve unit of the JNA before the war started?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in military maneuvers, and that's how I was connected with that person or those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now please tell me when you attended that military maneuver. You were a member of a unit, right, and that unit was a reserve unit of the JNA. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was at the time the so-called Territorial Defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was a part of the JNA. That's how things were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that they all wore the same uniforms? There was not much difference between the Territorial Defence units and the reserve units.

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by and large I can agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time in the Territorial Defence units and in the reserve forces of the JNA, there were members of all nations and they were all residents of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the crisis started and led up to the war, did the Territorial Defence units and the reserve units of the JNA disintegrate due to their mixed composition? They did not stick together, as it were.

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those possibilities are now being psychologically reconsidered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, did the units remain the same as they were in 1986 or 1987? Did they continue being the same in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the new state emerged things changed in all aspects, including the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the units that you were a member of? I am talking about that reserve unit that you were a member of? Did it remain the same, was it transformed; hence, you joined another unit?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: We were only called when there were military maneuvers; i.e., we did not have a full and permanent assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you attended a military maneuver you were a member of a unit, were you not?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all members of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Every time when you were called to attend a manoeuvre, were you always a member of one in the same unit? Did you always attend with the same people?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you it was a changeable form, which means that not all the people are always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to put just a couple of questions to you that relate to Ovcara and your surrender or your arrest. The way I understood you was this: Up to the moment when a soldier of the JNA appeared in the hangar at Ovcara and took your details, nobody had created any lists, for example, in the hospital or in the JNA barracks while you were sitting on the buses and waiting?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Nobody made a list of our names. I was on a list of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. During that period of time from the arrival of the JNA at the hospital to the moment when you were transported to Ovcara and from Ovcara, did you see JNA members with white belts?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that those people took us out from the hangar, but I am not sure at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I will move on to the interrogation in Sid. You said that you were brought to a police station, to the civilian police station in Sid and that you were interrogated there by a civilian. Since you were in the civilian police station and since you were interrogated by a civilian, is that why you concluded that he was a SUP inspector?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That was my personal conclusion. He did not introduce himself. He did not wear a police uniform. Since he came to the premises, I thought that he was an inspector because that's how he comported himself and he interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will repeat the question. On that occasion did he tell you -- when he said that he had seen you at Ovcara, did he tell you where he had seen you, in the hangar, in front of the bus, on the bus? Did he tell you anything more precise than that?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now just one more thing, I need your clarification. You told him that you didn't know anything about Ovcara, that you didn't know him, that you had not seen him before. What I would like to know is this: Is it really true that you did not see him at Ovcara, that you didn't notice him, or perhaps you did but you kept quite about that for understandable reasons?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that I didn't know anything about Ovcara. I just denied the knowledge of the number of people who were killed at Ovcara. In that conversation when we stopped talking, that was that, and we did not discuss the place where he saw me or where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a lot of background noise in the headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, you denied that you saw him at Ovcara and he claimed that he had seen you?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he saw and where he saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were at Ovcara, you really did not see him or remember him as having been there?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing that I am interested in and it is about the blockade of the JNA barracks in Vukovar. Do you know why the barracks was blockaded, why there was no electricity, why there was no water, why the supply of food was interrupted for JNA members who were there?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. As far as I know, the barracks had a permanent communication with one of the sides to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that it could remain having those permanent contacts via radio?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the physical blockade of the barracks because that blockade was one-side as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be all, Witness. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Demirdjian, re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, I have two small questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us about your family being prevented from return to Vukovar in August 1991, and you said that your family was prevented from returning to Vukovar at a place called Kutina. Can you please tell us who or on whose authority the convoy was prevented from returning, and how did you know this?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the convoys were stopped by the MUP and other bodies of that executive power because the shelling of Vukovar started, and I heard that over the phone because there was still phone communications working at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You also stated, sir, it was on 5 March, page 3339 of the transcript, that you were transported from the hospital in Vukovar to the JNA barracks in Vukovar, and that you saw there were reservists and soldiers at the barracks when you arrived. I suppose that when you said "soldiers," you mean JNA soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Those soldiers were JNA members. But there were also reservists as members of the JNA, so it was a joint form of resistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And how did you make the difference between reservists and soldiers? I mean, did you -- did they wear -- did they have different uniforms or insignia, whatever?

utterances.speaker: GH-080 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was precisely what was difficult. It was very difficult to say who was a regular soldier and who was a reservist, and especially that applied to those who had different uniforms or partially different uniforms, and that was an additional difficulty in making a distinction between them. But, as a matter of fact, it was a joint form of people who worked in concert, they had their commanders, they had their generals [as interpreted] of supervision and organisation, and in my mind there was no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no other questions arising from this, then, Mr. Witness, this brings your testimony to the -- your testimony to an end. We thank you very much for your -- Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just notice one unclear point in the transcript. The witness said that "they had different channels of supervision and organisation," and here is "generals of supervision." It is line 19, page 8. There, "generals," he said "channels."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Mr. Witness, that you said that "they had their channels of supervision and organisation?" Was that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the gist of that was that there were different channels through which they exercised supervision. I believe that they were supervised from different sides, but I don't think that it is up to me to provide more comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the witness did say "channels" in his first answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, we thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. The Court Usher will escort you out of court as soon as we are in closed session, and we wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Demirdjian, your -- the next witness is a viva voce witness, no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, Your Honours. However Ms. Dennehy will be coming in. She will be the attorney taking next witness, so I will excuse myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Mr. Registrar, we don't need a break for the setting? No. It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As soon as counsel for the Prosecution is here, we will bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's my assumption, Your Honour. I'd actually expected the personnel to be here from 9.00, but that hasn't happened, unfortunately. Your Honour, before the witnesses brought in, just to let the record reflect that the Prosecution is now represented by Ms. Muireann Dennehy and our legal intern, August Sommerfeld, who just entered courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Dennehy. Glad to see you up and running so soon in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for my delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. Can you state your first and last name, your date of birth, and your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 24th of November, 1955, in Vukovar. My name is Branko Culic. I am Croat by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses comitted themselves to tell the truth. I point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Would you now mistake the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Ms. Dennehy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, can you please tell the Court where you live at the moment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I live in Vukovar at present.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What part of Vukovar do you live in? What part specifically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: In the area which is on Budzak Street, near the Dzerge forest, on the road to Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And would you describe this area as near or close to Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The local commune I live in belongs to Vukovar but is on the boundary with Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in this area for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Ever since I was born and up until the homeland war in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what you did after you finished school?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I worked as a driver for the Cazmatrans transport company which transported passengers. This was a company that was stationed in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where did you receive your qualifications as a driver?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I obtained my qualifications in 1974 and 1975 when I did my compulsory military service, and then I got the B-category license later on in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And after working as a driver for the Cazmatrans company, what was your job after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I retrained and became the fire fighter and driver of the fire engine, and in 1989 I joined the fire brigade in Vukovar in that same capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Before joining the Vukovar fire brigade, did you ever work as a bus driver?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was a bus driver before I joined the professional fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what villages did you drive the bus in?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I started driving the bus, I covered the Vukovar-Pacetin route for six years.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did you first meet Goran Hadzic, the accused?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I met Goran Hadzic in 1980. He came to my house to see my dog, a German shepherd who was of a very good pedigree.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you ever have occasion to go to Pacetin and see Goran Hadzic there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Since I had that bus route to cover, I had time to take off my duty and go to his home and see his German shepherd that he had at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what was your involvement with the football teams in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: On some days I was assigned to drive the footballers of the Pacetin Sloga team when they had matches away from home, and that would normally be on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And was Goran Hadzic part of that football team?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: He was a member of that football team. He was a footballer.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now moving onto the Croatian declaration of independence, how did that declaration of independence in 1991 increase the tensions between Serbs and Croats in the area that you were living?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: As far as my understanding goes and as far as I was able to follow, when the League of Communists of Yugoslavia disintegrated in Belgrade, the various republics of Yugoslavia saw democratic processes begin, leading to the emergence of new political parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you observe any tensions between Serbs and Croats at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: There were no tensions before the emergence of new political parties with their respective platforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what practical changes did you see in the police force as a result of the changes that took place at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When the HDZ won in Croatia, I heard from the people I lived with that some of the Serbs refused to wear a chequer-board as a symbol on their hat or cap.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And around this time, did you know of any barricades that were being set up in the area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The barricades emerged in the spring of 1991 - was it April or May, I'm not sure - but that was first in Serbian villages. They were the first ones to erect barricades.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what were the names of those Serbian villages that erected barricades?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Those were the villages with the majority Serb population, Brsadin, Borovo Selo, Bobota, Pacetin, Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who patrolled those barricades in the villages that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Now, whether there were some groups of people in specific villages who took upon that role, I don't know. At any rate, they were Serbs and they manned these barricades and were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were these local Serbs or were they Serbs from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: From what I know, they were from elsewhere. The Novi Sad TV broadcast footages of the barricades manned by the Serbs and I learnt that there was a certain number of them who had come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you have a term for those Serbs who came from Serbia in particular?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Amongst ourselves we would say that the Chetniks from Serbia had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court what happened to your brother-in-law at one of these Serb barricades?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Zlatko Rihter, from Celija, a small Croat village, was headed to Pacetin to see the veterinarian technician because his cow had had calves and he wanted him to visit his farm. He wasn't aware of the fact that there were barricades. And at the barricades on the way to Pacetin, on the edge of Pacetin, he was stopped and he was threatened. One of them I knew for sure but I can't recall his name, he placed the point of his rifle in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for erecting the Serb barricades around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court how did the Croats react to the Borovo Selo incident in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When on the 2nd of May, 1991, a massacre occurred in Borovo Selo against the Croatian police, among those of us Croats who were in Borovo Naselje, from what I could gather, fear spread.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did the Croats in the area do as a result of this fear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The various local communes started organising themselves. Or, rather, the Croats started organising themselves in these local communes, and slowly they would stand guard on the streets. And I can vouch for my local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when say the local communes starting organising themselves, what do you mean specifically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that they were afraid and they wanted to check the movement of people to know who precisely was passing down the street. We were afraid of the Serb rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now you told us earlier that you worked as a fire fighter Vukovar, and can you please tell me where did you work during the summer of 1991 until the 5th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Where did you work after the Borovo Selo incident in May until October 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I worked in the professional fire brigade every day. I had to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did your work involve with the fire brigades?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I was on duty and if there was fire anywhere I had to go out into the field and intervene. So I had to be on duty within the fire brigade station in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And during this time, did you ever have to visit Vukovar Hospital as part of your job as a fire fighter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The first and the last time I was at the Vukovar Hospital was on the 5th of October, 1991, when I brought 10.000 litres of water together with my colleague fire fighter, Slobodan Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you visited the hospital on the 5th of October, what did you see in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Since the shelling was heavy, we made sure that the water decanted into the apposite container, and I went into the basement where I saw a crowd of wounded who were lying in beds, some of them unconscious. The stench was unbearable and I didn't know where it was that I was worse off, down there with them or upstairs where the shells were landing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you continue to work as a fire fighter after the 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: No, I escaped from the fire brigade station when the tanks reached all the way to the station. We dispersed and I went home.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you say the tanks reached the station, what tanks were those?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: They were the tanks of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did you do after the fire brigade station was attacked by the JNA tanks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: All the members of the fire brigade who were in the station dispersed and fled across the graveyard to -- in the direction of the centre of town -- of town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in the days after the tanks attacking the fire brigade, what did you do during those days? Did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to work anymore. My car had been destroyed first and then my motor as well, so I stayed at home at Budzak where I manned the position opposite the Dzerge forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what position was this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Budzak is on the edge of Vukovar. When travelling from Vinkovci, along that road you will come across the Budzak Street which is right by the Dzerge forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you say "the position," was that a military position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: That was our defence line at the time. At Budzak, opposite the Dzerge forest, the rebel Serbs and perhaps some other paramilitaries were in the Dzerge forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what happened on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, we retreated from that position and went to the Borovo complex to the shelter where women and children were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 6231 - that's tab 16 of the Court's bundle - be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you'll shortly see a document on the screen in front of you. Mr. Culic, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What is this a document -- a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The photograph depicts an area of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please mark with an X where you were stationed at Budzak Street?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please tell me where do you live in relation to the place that you've just marked with an X?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I marked the house where I stayed until the very end. That -- that was where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please mark with a Y the Borovo factory complex. Or if you can just circle the factory complex for me, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this annotated version of the photograph 65 ter 6231 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1408. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Culic. Now, you've told us on the 18th of November you retreated into the Borovo factory complex that you've just indicated on the map -- or the photograph, I apologise. Can you please describe what you saw when you entered the Borovo factory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at the shelter of the Borovo factory, my late father, my step-mother, and two neighbours with their children were already there. It was on the night between the 18th and the 19th that I arrived at the footwear workshop. I was with them until the 20th, when we surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were inside the factory complex when you retreated into it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: In that basement where I arrived and where my family were, there were around a thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 4799.8 be shown. That's a video. That's at tab 14 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you will shortly see a video being played on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have just a moment, please. Mr. President, I've been advised that the transcript is in e-court and it is available at present. I apologise that it hasn't been given to the interpreters before now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, do you need the clip for the images only or for images and the spoken bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: For this particular exhibit, Mr. President, I only need the images. I do not need the sound. However, for other videos that I intend to play there are transcripts, I believe, available, and I will be tendering transcripts as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we can continue with this clip for the images only.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And you make sure that the transcripts are with the interpreters when you play the next one.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, the scenes in front of you on the video we've just played, do you recognise those scenes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell me where are these scenes from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I can't see anything on the screen at the moment. I see myself. Can you change that? I can't see the thing that you want me to see. I have nothing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that the video again be shown - that's Exhibit 4799.8 - in order to let the witness see the images.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Again, can you please tell me where are these scenes from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: This was taken in the new shoe factory in the basement or in the area known as atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And was this part of the factory complex where you took shelter and where you were treated to after the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That room was within the perimeter of the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this video, 4799.8, be admitted into evidence, images only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1409. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, so we remove the transcript from e-court, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: For this particular clip, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For this more clip, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you mentioned earlier that you surrender on the 20th of November, 1991, can you please describe for the Court what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: On the 20th November, 1991, in the shoe factory of the Borovo complex, an officer came to the gate. He was a highly-ranked officer of the JNA, either lieutenant-colonel or colonel. He was accompanied by the military police. He came to the gate of the Borovo complex. A group of some 20 or 30 men, defenders who had withdrawn into the complex, approached them and they started talking. Zeljko Jukic was amongst us. He immediately recognised the officer in question because they had known each other from before. Zeljko Jukic was his orderly in the army in Novi Sad. They started talking. He said, Please organise yourself as soon as possible and surrender as soon as possible. I cannot suppress [Realtime transcript read in error, "express"] the Chetniks any longer. They will storm in.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I ask -- can I ask that the record be amended.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I believe the transcript reads, "I cannot express." I believe the witness says, "I cannot repress [sic]."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Suppress," the interpreter notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, other than the negotiations between Zeljko Jukic and the lieutenant-colonel of the JNA on that day, were you aware of any other negotiations that took place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I was down in the shelter I heard, and later on I checked, that Ivica Banovic, the guards' commander and the police commander from Varazdin, and another commander, Filkovic, went to Borovo Selo to negotiate the future surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who did Banovic and Filkovic negotiate with at Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: They negotiated with a highly ranking JNA officer and Arkan who was also there, the notorious Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: So going back to your surrender at the Borovo factory on the 20th, what were you and the other Croat forces ordered to do with your weapons when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: It was agreed that colonel, lieutenant-colonel said that those of us who were armed had to surrender their weapons, that we would be checked, and what he had in mind were the defenders. And then we would be put on buses and taken to camps. Civilians, on the other hand, women and children, would be on a -- the other side and they would be taken to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that the lieutenant-colonel said he could not suppress the Chetniks. What other forces, and Serb forces in particular, were present at the factory that day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: There was a certain number of tanks at the very entrance to the Borovo complex.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were there other armed Serb forces present?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: At the moment when we surrendered on the other side of the fence, there were all sorts of formations including the JNA as well as people with Chetnik markings on them. There were also people with stars on their hats. There were all sorts of formations but their numbers were not large.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of those formations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. We called some the White Eagles or Arkan's Men or rebel Serbs or the JNA. That's how we called them. When I say the JNA, I mean the regular JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now ask that exhibit number 4798.4 be shown. That's at tab 10 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you'll shortly see another video on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: In order to assist the Court's interpreters, may I ask that this be shown again. I do believe the transcript is also available in respect of this video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes, we have not been provided with a hard copy of the transcript, and without it we cannot interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We need to provide the interpreters with a hard copy, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we do that right away?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I am told that the hard copy transcripts are on their way. It may take another few moments. Perhaps it's best if I leave this and I can continue on and show the video once the transcripts have been provided to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It seems a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, we are going to show that particular video and others shortly. There has been a procedural delay and so we will go back to that video. In the meantime, I'd like you to tell the Court what happened after you surrendered to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I surrendered my weapons, I was searched and then I got on a bus. I was on the bus number 2 or number 3 and the defenders Vukovar were there together with me. I was waiting to be taken into an unknown. I didn't know where we would be taken to.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what happened to the civilians who were present at the Borovo factory at the same time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: We were looking towards the gate. We were on the left side and they were on the right side. We were put on buses, whereas at the same time they were put on trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now you said you were on bus number 2 or 3 with the other defenders of Vukovar. Where were you and the other men brought to after you left the Borovo factory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: We drove through Borovo, Trpinja, at the Bobota-Vera cross-roads, and then we turned right. We drove through Vera, we arrived in Bogojevo, we crossed the bridge, and we entered Vojvodina. From Bogojevo, we were taken directly to Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did the JNA tell you about where you were going when the buses left Borovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The military policemen, members of the JNA who searched us, we knew some of them from before. They told us that nothing would happen to us, that we would be taken to a camp. That's what a military policeman told us. None of the other military personnel told us anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When my bus pulled over in front of Stajicevo, and let me tell you I was wounded in the right arm, that's -- that was a very difficult period of my life. I'd never experienced anything like that before or after. I'd run a gauntlet and a military jeep lights shone straight into our eyes, and in the gauntlet there were JNA military police who beat us. So we did not see who it was who beat us because we were blinded by the jeep lights.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did the JNA military police beat you with as you ran through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Some beat us with their hand. Some kicked us. Some had batons. Some had wooden sticks.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Did you see any women being beaten when you arrived at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The first and last time in my life I saw that. On the left-hand side a military police officer spotted a woman in a military uniform, and he said, Look at this ZNG lass. And he hit her so she fell down on the floor. It was a terrible thing to do. It was an awful moment, something that I'll remember all my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you saw when you arrived at Stajicevo? Or can you -- let me rephrase that: Can you please describe the building into which you entered when you arrived at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: It was a longish building. It was a cattle barn. In the middle there was an opening about 2 metres wide and on both sides there were boxes for cows. As we entered, we were shouted at, we were beaten, they directed those lights at us, and they instructed us to lie down on the floor and that we should not lift our heads. There was commotion and chaos. There was dogs there as well. It was like in a movie. I don't know if you have ever seen any movie about Auschwitz, but if you did, I can tell you that it was exactly like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were housed in the stable that you just described?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: About a thousand, give or take. I'm sure that there was a thousand of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you first entered the building, were there any men there or people before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When we first entered, we saw that there were people there, not many. They had arrived before us, one day or one night before us. But I realised that only later. I was so afraid. They shouted at us. I could not focus on anything else. When they shouted "sit down" or "lie down" that's what I did. I wasn't looking around.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you said "when they shouted" at you, who do you mean? Who shouted at you and who was guarding you at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: At Stajicevo there were JNA military police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you know who was in charge of the camp at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: On the following day, during the course of that day a person entered the barn and introduced himself. He told us his name and he said that he was the commander of the camp, and he said that we were prisoners, that we were war rebels. He said that he -- that we would be interrogated, that the conditions of our stay would improve. That's what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And to what part of the military did this commander belong?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I don't know who he was. In any case, he wore a uniform. He sported some insignia. I don't know what his rank was. I know that he was a JNA officer and he introduced himself to us as the person in charge, the one who was responsible for that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Court how the JNA military police ordered you to sit or stand while you were at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: In any case they shouted. They used bad words. They would shout "heads down," and then they would hit us by batons. Usually by batons. They told us that we had to obey them. That we should not look at them. That we should not lift our heads. They wanted to make sure that we understood that since we were there that it was not a good thing for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Culic, you said that the JNA commander of the camp said that you were war rebels. Were you charged with any crime at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: No. Never. I was never prosecuted for any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and before I show the next exhibit I wondered whether now would be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We still have four minutes, but if that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask in that case that 65 ter 2410.1 be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you'll soon see a document on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: This is tab 6 of the Court's binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, at the bottom left corner of that document, do you see a circle marked in red?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, did you make this circle marked in red while at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did you make this marking on this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court why you circled in red the number at the bottom left corner of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Because I recognised the names of some people who were in Stajicevo with me. I know some of them by name and the others I know by sight. I know their faces but I can't put any names to those faces unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, the name that you have circled, Barbir, was that person in Stajicevo when you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I please ask that this document, 65 ter 2410.1, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1410. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ready for a break now, Ms. Dennehy?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, we will take the first break now, come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, just before the break you looked at a document that you had marked yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that the Court Officer bring up Exhibit P1410. Can I please scroll to the next page, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you indicated before the break that you had circled certain numbers indicating that those names were those individuals who were at Stajicevo with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now looking at the document in front of you, can you please name the individual who you have circled and who was at Stajicevo with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: On this sheet I only circled the name of Ivan Batarelo. I know that there are more of them by the last name of Batarelo, but I know that he was with me at Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can we please scroll through to the next indicated name.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, can you please indicate the names that appear in front of you now as those individuals who were at Stajicevo with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I circled Bozo Brekalo, Damir Brnas, Ivan Brnas, father and son, another Ivan Brnas. There were three or four of them. They were all family. I don't know if they were cousins. At any rate, they were related. Then I also circled Ivan Budim, who was a mechanic at Cazmatrans. I also circled Miroslav Budim, his son. I circled the name of Josip Budimir. He was a neighbour of mine. Filip Budimir, his brother. Zoran Capan was a young man living on the street next to mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, what ethnicity were the people who you just named are, the people you just named?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: All those who -- whom I've mentioned just now were Croats. Some of them may have been from mixed families, Serb or Hungarian, but most of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask the Court Officer now to scroll through to the page that is the last page of this exhibit that is marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Culic, on page 23 of this document in front of you, can you please name the people who you have indicated were in Stajicevo with you on this page, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Robert Zivkovic, Sandor Zivkovic, Simo Zivkovic, Boris Zuvela. I don't know these people as well as I do the others, but I know that they were ...

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Were those people in Stajicevo with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Based on what is written here and from what I remember, I believe that they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: So if I can ask you that question again, from what you remember were those people at Stajicevo with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, those persons were with me at Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Culic, what ethnicity, if you know, were these people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: As for the Zivkovic family, I don't think that they are Croats. I do believe that Boris Zuvela [Realtime transcript read in error "Zivkovic"] is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Culic, we are going to show you a number of videos that we mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If I could please ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interruption, but I think it is an error in transcript. He said "Boris Zuvela," not "Boris Zivkovic." It is line 7, page 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you confirm that, Mr. Witness, who you believe was a Croat, Boris, what's his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads Zuvela and it's a well-known family name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now please ask that 65 ter 4798.4 be shown. That's a video at tab 10 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] You can get involved a bit here to help to get these people pull out, those wounded over there. "A decisive action of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army with the particular distinction of the Zrenjanin Battalion as they called it, the decisive attack against this Ustasha stronghold was carried out. This afternoon, around 5.00 p.m., the resistance has finally been broken; the members of MUP and ZNG have raised their hands up in the air. Approximately a thousand of them surrendered."

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, do you recognise the scenes on the video that we've just shown you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what are these scenes of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: These scenes show how the Komerc building, which was part of the Borovo complex, and the people who were in that building surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what -- you saw a building burning in this video, what building is that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: This was the Komerc building which was in fact a storage place for the finished products.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you know who the men lining up against the wall at the very end of the video, do you know who those men are?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Most of them were defenders of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And finally, the scenes that you've just seen on the video, are they reminiscent of the day that you surrendered at the Borovo factory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Our surrender within the Borovo complex was a bit more organised. We were recorded on a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I ask that this Exhibit, 65 ter 4798.4, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1411. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, I am going to show you another video.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 4789.3 - that's at tab 8 - be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: ... a factory near Vukovar where the Croats had held out until the last. The army was rounding up a thousand civilians and 500 former soldiers. There is a massive and forced migration of people going on. Again, each side is charging the other with atrocities. The facts are unclear, but some terrible things were done in the final hours. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, from the video I've just shown, do you recognise the scenes on that video?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what are those scenes of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: They were the people again who had surrendered in the complex of the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And did you recognise any of the men in that video?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who were those men that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I recognised a young man. I can't recall his name. He was and electrician at Cazma. On the 20th in the morning when I brought over the water tanker, the Komerc building was empty, I drove over the water tanker to connect it to the building so that people would have water. I asked the officer who was there to allow me to drive the water tanker through because people were thirsty. He charged a soldier to accompany me and make sure that I wouldn't escape. I recognised that soldier in the footage here. He helped me connect the water tanker after I had driven it over.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And the man that you recognise in the video, what uniform is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: He didn't have a uniform. He was there for the purposes of the shelter where the women and children were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can we please show the video again in order for the witness to identify the men who he's speaking of.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: ... and at a factory near Vukovar where the Croats had held out to the last. The army was rounding up a thousand civilians and 500" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the young man I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: ... spend the night. And at a factory near Vukovar, where the Croats had held up until last. The army was rounding up a thousand civilians and 500" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the lad that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And Mr. Culic, do you recognise the next man who is shown in the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, wouldn't it be good to have on the record the exact reference in the clip?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. Please let the record show that at time stamp 25:29:5, the witness has identified an unnamed man who he knows from the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: ... former soldiers. There is a massive and forced migration of people going on. Again, each side the charging the other with atrocities. The facts are unclear, but some terrible things were done in the final hours. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that 65 ter 4789.3, the video that's just been shown, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1412. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And may I now show - and this is the last video for the time being - the exhibit at 65 ter 4799.7. That's tab 13 of the Court's bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Miodrag Popov: Today, again around 700 Ustashas have surrendered, amongst them also the well known leaders of the Zenge, ZNG members, and members of the MUP from this area. They were hiding deep underground, in cellars and catacombs of the Borovo company. It is obvious that during the last months this company, which was once a Yugoslav company, was turned into a nest of Croatian Ustashas."

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, do you recognise the scenes from the video that have been just shown to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what are these the scenes of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I recognise the shelter where I spent one day and where my late father, my step-mother, and my neighbours were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I ask that this video be shown again and it be paused at time stamp 55:30.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, from the scene and the image that is shown to you now, do you recognise these buses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And why do you recognise these buses?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Because we boarded the buses, and I mean the defenders who were on the right-hand side. We boarded the buses and we were told that we were being taken to camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 4799.7, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1413. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Culic, I'd like to move back to before the break when we spoke and you told the Court about your detention at the camp, Stajicevo. Were you interrogated while you were at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated only once.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who interrogated you while you were at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: A military policeman of the JNA. And at the barn where we were held, he read out my first and last name and took me out of the barn into a house and a room inside it. I had to keep my head bowed and I couldn't look where we were going, and he, in fact, took me to an interrogator, an official.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of your interrogation at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: When I got there, he asked me to raise my head and asked me when I was born. I told him that I was born on the 24th of November, 1955, and he told me, Well, you've just celebrated your birthday. How are you doing? And I said, Fine. I didn't dare say anything else. He asked me where I was deployed, at which positions, what sort of weapons did I have, did I fire from those weapons, and if I know knew anything about any crimes. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How were you and the other men treated by the guards at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The JNA military policemen at the Stajicevo camp treated us so roughly, shouted at us, beat us, and humiliated us in such a manner as I had never experienced in my life before. I so frightened that I didn't dare eat anything for days at an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How did -- you've just mentioned that the JNA military police "beat us." Can you describe that for the Court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: We were in the shed or the barn and lined into two lines. They would pass in the aisle in the middle - they had those German shepherds initially, the dogs - and beat us. Whoever dared raise his head a bit would be beaten immediately. So nobody dared rear their heads. That was in the early days. They terrorised us and they just walked past us and beat whomever they pleased. We were lying down on the concrete. It was terrible. If I may continue, whenever we had to go to the toilet, we would raise our hand and allowed to go. I am talking about the first days of the our time at Stajicevo. We went out to do whatever we needed to do, to pass water. They would always be insulting us and abusing us. It was horrible to even look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How did they abuse you when you asked to go outside?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I will demonstrate this. I would raise my hand like this and say I have to go to the toilet, and then I would stand up and be on my way. But as soon as you were on your way, they would beat you. And then if you were passing water, as you were doing that, and urinating, they would be beating you. So they wouldn't leave us in peace even in those moments. That was at the beginning. It was horrid to even look at when other people were being abused this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Did any of the prisoners die while you were at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The early days at Stajicevo, there were people who were of a poor mind state and simply didn't know what they were doing anymore. They lost it. And they would stand up and start running somewhere. And, of course, we weren't allowed to do anything, not even look up, unless you were given permission. So whoever dared stand up uncontrollably, they would immediately swarm him and beat him, kick him and punch him. There was this case involving Kunac, a man who used to live on a street next to mine. He lost it and they jumped him, beat him up. They never stopped and he died later. That was 10 metres away from me. He was five years older than me and went to school with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when you say "they" jumped him, beat him up. Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear enough. Those were military policemen. They were always there. They were the rulers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross visit you while you were at Stajicevo camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross did come to visit once, as far as I remember. That was on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did the Red Cross do when they visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: We were relieved to see them because we knew that they would make a list of all of our names. Our numbers would be known. That was a guarantee that they would not take us away into an unknown. That was very important, for our names to be known, and for us to send messages to our families if we knew where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Did you complain to the Red Cross delegates when they visited Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I did not have to complain. They realised and they knew, they saw the conditions that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now ask that 65 ter 2407.1 - that's at tab 4 - be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, you'll shortly see a document on the screen in front of you. Mr. Culic, can you -- do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What is this a document of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: This is a document containing the names of those people who were at Stajicevo with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the red markings on this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And who made those red markings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: When did you make those markings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And why did you make those markings on the [indiscernible] document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I made them because I recognised the names of some of the people who were at Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court at number 158, who is the individual who is shown on this list?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: 158 is Dr. Emedi, a physician who dressed my wounds at Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where was this doctor from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: He was from Vukovar, he resided in Vukovar, and he worked as a doctor in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this exhibit, 65 ter 2407.1 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1414. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I now ask that 65 ter 4986.2, that's a video, at tab 15 of the Court's bundle, be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Unknown man 1: They butchered everything that moved. That's how it was. "Unknown man 2: This is the famous Yugoslav factory of rubber and footwear factory, Borovo. Some 1.000 to 1500 Croatian soldiers surrendered here today. "Petar Mlinaric: I can show you the place where I was separated and put on a bus with people I have never seen again. Bearded people came. They didn't know us anymore. "Mirko Kovacic: Everything is as it was. "Unknown woman 1: Don't cry. Please don't cry. "Mirko Kovacic: We arrived here on the 19th around midnight. There were eight buses. I was in the third bus. This is where the gauntlet was, where they beat us."

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, the building that you saw at the end of this video, what was that building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I have nothing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that the video be shown again for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we object to the -- we let it go the first time because it started before I realised what was being presented. What we have is an audio of individuals who were witnesses to this event that are being put to the witness. This is precisely the same as if we have, for example, a statement given to anyone some years after the events that are then read to the witness. And as you know, I tried to do this just on Monday and was told that wasn't permissible. And I understand why that is. But, nonetheless, that's what we're doing now. The Prosecution is putting a statement by witnesses to these events and then asking for the witness to comment upon that. So just in terms of what the remedy would be, no objection to showing the images, but there is an objection to putting the -- this -- essentially this testimony of witnesses to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, any reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution does not intend to put this witness testimony to this particular witness. The purpose of this video evidence is to identify the detention sites that the witness was present at. Therefore, if it pleases the Court, we can tender or suggest to tender this video without either the transcript or sound, merely for the images that it presents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if I understand, Mr. Gosnell, that the clip will be tendered for the images only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the issue isn't only the admission, the tendering, the issue is whether it should be put to the witness, the audio. And what we see now is the audio is being put to the witness and then the witness is supposed to give a comment or a reaction. I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But not on the audio. Not on what is said. Only on the images.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, it -- but if the images are -- sorry, if the audio is played, whatever questions are asked, it's going to be inevitably infected by whatever was heard on the audio, and I thought that that was precisely what the Chamber considered objectionable in respect of statements being read verbatim into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Chamber didn't rule on the objection a few days ago, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's true you didn't rule, but you did direct me not to read the statement in question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the spot we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I duly did not read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, without taking a position on whether or not, can we show -- can we show the video without the audio? This is a question to the OTP or to the Registrar? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can show just the images only and not the audio of this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And then I suppose remove the transcript from e-court. Is that what you wanted to say, Mr. Registrar? Or is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll show it again without the audio.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've also been asked to inform you that the witness, to the Prosecution's knowledge, does not speak English and therefore cannot read the subtitles that are contained on this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, from the images that have just been shown to you, do you recognise these images?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: From the building that has just been shown to you, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I recognise the building. I will never forget it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court where is that building?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: That building is near Zrenjanin, on a farm, and the name of that farm is Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And was this the detention facility that you were detained at, at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where we from Vukovar were detained. That's -- that was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And Mr. Culic, the image in front of you now, at time stamp 1:36:51.2, do you recognise those scenes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: The barbed wire that you see in the video, was that the barbed wire that you surrounded the Stajicevo camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: That barbed wire surrounded the camp and there were guards at every corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If we can now continue the video until time stamp 36:56, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, do you recognise these scenes as being similar to those that you experienced at Stajicevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And everything is similar to when I was at Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can we now play the remainder of the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that this 65 ter 4986.2 be admitted into evidence, images only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marking.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit P1415. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. Culic, how long were you detained at Stajicevo for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Stajicevo for a month, give or take. In any case, around a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did you leave Stajicevo, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
utterances.text: We left Stajicevo before the Catholic Christmas that year, before the 24th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how many men left Stajicevo on the day that you left?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO CULIC
